lessons.shortName: Die-to-die links and UCIe compatibility
lessons.role: Defines what adjacent chiplets must agree on to exchange useful data.
lessons.description: A package link connects separately manufactured logic regions through short wires and interfaces. A common standard can define electrical behavior, link training and supported protocols, but compatibility still depends on the selected package class, widths, rates and implementation options. UCIe’s public explanation describes negotiation of operating parameters during initialization. The physical link must also fit the package routing and power budget. A label saying UCIe therefore identifies a framework for interoperability rather than proving that any two purchased chiplets can be assembled together without additional design and qualification work.

lessons.name: PCIe and CXL: transport versus memory semantics
lessons.shortName: PCIe and CXL
lessons.role: Distinguishes peripheral data transfer from supported coherent memory operations.
lessons.description: PCI Express provides a widely used physical and protocol foundation for host devices. CXL builds on a PCIe physical foundation while adding defined cache and memory semantics alongside I/O. This enables supported devices to participate in coherent access or expose memory through specific host/device roles. It does not make distant memory equivalent to local DRAM: requests still cross links, queues and controllers. Software, firmware and device generation determine what is actually enabled. A diagram should show both the physical route and the ownership or coherence behavior, because equal link rates do not imply identical programming semantics.

specs.label: Memory expansion
specs.context: Capacity does not guarantee local-memory latency or bandwidth.

lessons.tradeoff: Expanded or shared memory can improve capacity utilization while exposing link latency and management complexity.
lessons.whyAI: Model state that does not fit near an accelerator may use a larger memory tier, but traffic-sensitive operations need a measured access budget.

lessons.name: Signal integrity, timing and the eye diagram
lessons.shortName: Signal integrity, timing and the eye diagram
lessons.role: Tests whether a receiver can distinguish transmitted symbols under actual channel conditions.
lessons.description: A digital link uses analog voltages or currents to encode symbols. Wires, connectors and package transitions attenuate and distort those signals; neighboring activity and supply noise add interference. A receiver needs enough voltage separation and timing margin to decide correctly. An eye diagram overlays many symbol intervals to reveal the available opening, while bit-error measurements test actual outcomes under stated conditions. Equalization can compensate for some channel loss but adds complexity and power. The IBM BoW interface study is a concrete example of signal and power analysis tied to a particular package implementation.

specs.label: Eye opening
specs.context: Volts and seconds at a stated measurement point.

specs.label: Error rate
specs.context: Test duration and statistical confidence matter, especially with no observed errors.

interfaces.name: Transmitter and channel
interfaces.signal: Symbols distorted by channel loss, reflections and crosstalk

interfaces.name: Receiver decision
interfaces.signal: Recovered symbols and observed error events

lessons.tradeoff: Higher signaling rate or denser routing can raise bandwidth while reducing margin; equalization and extra spacing cost power or area.
lessons.whyAI: Correct arithmetic is useless if package or network links corrupt data, retry excessively or fail under high simultaneous activity.

lessons.name: Power integrity and transient voltage margin
lessons.shortName: Power integrity and transient voltage margin
lessons.role: Keeps the voltage at a chip within its operating window during changing current demand.
lessons.description: A voltage regulator supplies a target rail, but the chip sees that rail through resistive and inductive paths. A large current step can create both steady voltage drop and transient droop. Decoupling capacitors provide nearby charge while the regulator responds, yet their connections and resonances matter. Package power routing, board planes and regulator control must therefore be designed together. Power integrity differs from the facility’s annual energy budget: the critical event may last a tiny fraction of a second. A system can have ample nameplate power and still suffer timing errors or protective shutdowns during a fast load change.

specs.label: Voltage margin
specs.context: Upstream supply voltage does not establish die-local voltage.

specs.label: Impedance target
specs.context: Ohms over a frequency range, not one DC resistance alone.

interfaces.name: Regulator and distribution
interfaces.signal: Supply current through resistive/inductive paths

interfaces.name: Chip rail
interfaces.signal: Voltage with ripple, droop and recovery behavior

lessons.tradeoff: More capacitance and wider power paths can improve margin but consume space; aggressive load changes may require coordinated power control.
lessons.whyAI: Synchronized accelerator activity can create rapid current changes, making electrical dynamics relevant even when average power fits the rack budget.

lessons.name: A documented rack as a system boundary
lessons.shortName: A documented rack as a system boundary
lessons.role: Connects compute trays, switches, management, power and cooling in one named reference.
lessons.description: A rack-scale accelerator system contains more than GPUs. Compute trays hold CPUs, accelerators, local memory and peripheral devices; switches connect an acceleration domain; management controllers support configuration and recovery. Power shelves and busbars distribute electricity, while manifolds deliver coolant to selected components. NVIDIA’s DGX GB rack guide supplies a concrete NVL72 reference with distinct compute and switch trays. The reference is useful because its interfaces are documented, not because every AI installation uses this design. Selecting a tray should preserve its identity while the view changes between physical assembly, network communication, electricity and heat.

specs.context: Preserve generation and system configuration in any numeric card.

lessons.name: Scale-up, scale-out and management fabrics
lessons.shortName: Scale-up, scale-out and management fabrics
lessons.role: Assigns each traffic class to its actual interconnect and resource boundary.
lessons.description: Scale-up links connect tightly coupled accelerators within a selected domain, while scale-out networks join nodes or domains into larger clusters. Storage and management traffic may use separate fabrics even when cables or switches look similar. The distinction describes roles and locality, not a universal distance threshold or protocol monopoly. A collective can cross both domains, encountering different bandwidth, latency and contention. The NVIDIA rack documentation separates acceleration, cluster and management paths in a concrete implementation. A correct visualization follows the selected message across those boundaries and states whether any displayed bandwidth is one-way, bidirectional or an aggregate over many ports.

specs.context: Roles may share equipment but require separate accounting.

specs.context: A sum of ports is not a single flow’s achievable rate.

interfaces.signal: Messages crossing the required topology boundaries

lessons.name: Collective traffic and congestion
lessons.shortName: Collective traffic and congestion
lessons.role: Coordinates distributed tensor exchanges while accounting for topology and contention.
lessons.description: A collective describes communication among a group of participants. All-reduce combines values and returns the result to all ranks; all-gather assembles distributed pieces; reduce-scatter combines values while leaving different output pieces on different ranks. Libraries such as NCCL choose implementations suited to message size and topology. The logical collective is not identical to one physical link transfer. Congestion, competing storage traffic and poorly placed ranks can reduce useful bandwidth, while many small exchanges expose latency. Correct diagnosis follows both the operation’s semantics and the actual traffic schedule, including any communication that overlaps computation.

specs.label: Message size
specs.context: Do not confuse one rank’s input with total wire traffic.

specs.label: Effective bandwidth
specs.value: Useful bytes/s under the chosen algorithm
specs.context: Line rate omits protocol and contention losses.

interfaces.name: Rank-local tensors
interfaces.signal: Values requiring collection, distribution or reduction

interfaces.name: Collective output
interfaces.signal: Correctly placed combined or gathered tensors

lessons.tradeoff: Algorithms with fewer phases can help small messages, while larger transfers reward bandwidth-efficient routing; the best choice changes with topology.
lessons.whyAI: Synchronized training and tensor-parallel inference repeatedly wait for collective results, turning network behavior into model-step or token latency.

lessons.name: Optical transceivers and co-packaged optics
lessons.shortName: Optical transceivers and co-packaged optics
lessons.role: Changes where electrical signals become optical while retaining a complete link budget.
lessons.description: An optical link converts electrical data into modulated light, transports it through fiber and recovers an electrical signal at the destination. Pluggable transceivers put much of this conversion near a front-panel connector. Co-packaged optics moves optical engines closer to the switching silicon, shortening some high-speed electrical paths. The change can alter power, signal loss, thermal design, fiber attachment and serviceability. NVIDIA’s 2025 photonics announcement provides a named example. Optical networking is distinct from optical arithmetic: carrying tensor bytes with light does not mean the neural-network multiplication occurs in the optical link.

specs.label: Conversion boundary
specs.context: Near-package engines and pluggable modules have different maintenance paths.

specs.label: Optical budget
specs.context: Use a stated receiver requirement and wavelength; watts and dB describe different quantities.

interfaces.name: Switch electrical data
interfaces.signal: Serialized symbols and control to an optical engine

interfaces.name: Fiber receiver
interfaces.signal: Recovered payload after optical transport and detection

lessons.tradeoff: Shorter electrical paths can help signaling efficiency, while tighter packaging makes thermal isolation, fiber assembly and replacement planning more consequential.
lessons.whyAI: Large accelerator fabrics need many reliable links; link power and serviceability affect useful cluster uptime and infrastructure overhead.

lessons.name: Rack power conversion and distribution
lessons.shortName: Rack power conversion and distribution
lessons.role: Moves electrical energy from facility supply through conversion stages to low-voltage chip rails.
lessons.description: Facility electricity reaches a rack through distribution equipment and power supplies, then travels through busbars, board connections and local voltage regulators. Each stage has a voltage, current, capacity and conversion efficiency. The DGX GB reference describes power shelves converting AC to nominal rack DC, but other racks use different arrangements. Nameplate capacity includes redundancy and does not equal measured consumption. At the chip, low voltage implies high current for a given power, increasing the importance of short, low-resistance paths. A power-flow view must label its measurement location before turning watts into an estimate of available compute resources.

specs.context: Do not compare values from different locations as equivalent.

specs.context: Redundant supplies provide resilience and headroom, not automatic consumption.

interfaces.name: Chip voltage rails

lessons.whyAI: Accelerator deployment needs suitable distribution and regulation, not only enough annual electricity or enough power-supply labels.

lessons.role: Accounts for changes in electrical demand over timescales from chip activity to facility operation.
lessons.description: AI workloads alternate between arithmetic, communication, memory movement and idle intervals. Their electrical demand changes accordingly, and synchronized jobs can align changes across many devices. Power supplies, local decoupling, rack distribution and facility controls respond on different timescales. A daily energy total cannot reveal a fast voltage event, while a brief peak does not define annual energy. Power capping or workload scheduling can limit demand but may change completion time or service latency. The IEA discusses emerging power-system challenges from AI growth; a local engineering model must still use measured waveforms and the actual facility response.

lessons.name: Orbital solar generation and eclipse storage
lessons.shortName: Orbital solar generation and eclipse storage
lessons.role: Balances payload and spacecraft energy through sunlight, eclipse and degradation.
lessons.description: A solar-powered spacecraft must supply computation plus communications, control, thermal transport and other bus loads. Solar array output depends on illuminated area, conversion efficiency, orientation and degradation. An orbit with favorable sunlight can reduce eclipse demand, but sunlight is not the same as usable electricity and a sun-synchronous orbit is not automatically eclipse-free. Batteries cover intervals when generation falls below load and must later be recharged with losses included. NASA’s power-system guidance treats dynamic operating conditions and eclipse as design inputs. A compute scenario therefore needs a time-dependent energy ledger before declaring its solar area sufficient.

lessons.name: Radiators, view factors and orbital heat rejection
lessons.shortName: Radiators, view factors and orbital heat rejection
lessons.role: Rejects spacecraft waste heat through radiation while accounting for absorbed environmental heat.
lessons.description: Inside a spacecraft, conduction and fluid systems can move heat from electronics to a radiator. Outside, vacuum removes the ordinary air-convection path, so radiation is essential. A radiator emits according to temperature, area and emissivity, but also absorbs sunlight and radiation from Earth or nearby structures. Its view of the heat sink matters. NASA’s thermal-control guidance organizes this energy balance. Raising radiator temperature can reduce required emitting area while demanding higher allowable component temperatures or better heat transport. The coldness of deep space therefore does not make cooling free or guarantee that a dense compute payload can reject its heat.

lessons.tradeoff: Higher radiator temperature reduces area but consumes component thermal margin; shielding a radiator from sunlight constrains geometry and orientation.
lessons.whyAI: Nearly all consumed electrical power ultimately becomes heat, coupling compute intensity to radiator area and spacecraft mass.

NASA’s TBIRD demonstrated high-rate orbital downlink during particular passes, while Suncatcher’s disclosed high-rate result was a short ground bench path. Peak bit rate cannot be multiplied by a full day unless the link is actually usable for that whole interval. Data placement matters: processing a space-generated image locally may avoid much more traffic than serving a ground-resident training dataset.

lessons.role: Connects mission-specific particle exposure to device behavior and retained workload correctness.
lessons.description: Space radiation can accumulate damage over time or trigger immediate effects from individual particles. Total ionizing dose, displacement damage and single-event effects are different mechanisms and need different tests. A corrected memory error, a reboot, silent corruption and permanent damage also have different operational consequences. NASA’s radiation guidance emphasizes the environment and device response; Suncatcher provides a specific accelerator test example with important limits. Shielding changes exposure but adds mass and does not eliminate every particle mechanism. A useful computing service must detect unacceptable output changes and recover state, not merely keep an accelerator powered after irradiation.

lessons.role: Accounts for a computing fleet’s support mass and continuing lifecycle logistics.
lessons.description: An orbital payload launches with solar arrays, radiators, structure, communications, control and other support equipment. The relevant mass therefore includes far more than accelerator boards. Hardware degrades, fails or becomes obsolete, and physical repair may be limited by the mission design. A fleet needs spares, replenishment flights and a planned retirement path. NASA’s deorbit guidance describes physical disposal approaches whose suitability depends on orbit and spacecraft capabilities. Replacement cadence affects both sustained useful capacity and recurring launch demand. A low launch price per kilogram does not remove the need to manufacture, integrate and deploy every replacement system.

A scenario should show which assumptions make the budget close and which unresolved constraint prevents a useful service.

claims.title: NVL72 reference GPU count
claims.statement: The NVIDIA hardware guide describes 18 compute trays with four GPUs each in an NVL72 rack, totaling 72 GPUs.
claims.limitations: Inventory is not allocated capacity, measured throughput or one physical GPU die.

claims.title: Documented approximate rack consumption
claims.statement: The NVIDIA guide describes rack consumption as approximately 120 kW.
claims.denominator: per documented DGX GB reference rack
claims.scope: Rack consumption, separate from chip TDP and facility input
claims.limitations: Approximate configuration-specific value; PSU nameplate sum and actual workload draw differ.

claims.title: IEA estimated 2025 electricity demand
claims.statement: IEA’s April 2026 report estimates 485 TWh of worldwide data-center electricity demand in 2025.
claims.scope: All data centers, with AI-focused facilities a subset
claims.limitations: Estimated baseline, not an AI-only meter total or available power capacity.

claims.title: IEA central 2030 projection
claims.statement: IEA’s April 2026 central projection is 950 TWh of worldwide data-center electricity demand in 2030.
claims.scope: Same broad report scope as the separately labeled 2025 baseline
claims.limitations: Conditional projection, not observed consumption; not additive with US-only LBNL estimates.

claims.title: EuroHPC gigafactory procurement scope
claims.statement: The July 2026 EuroHPC call seeks up to seven AI gigafactories through a future selection process.
claims.scope: Proposed procurement scope, not operating facility count
claims.limitations: Do not combine with 19 AI factories being implemented or 13 access/support antennas as equivalent operating sites.

claims.title: Starcloud-1 reported accelerator demonstration
claims.statement: Starcloud reports a November 2025 launch carrying an H100 and a December 2025 nanoGPT training demonstration.
claims.period: November–December 2025, reported on living project page
claims.limitations: Not independent fleet reliability, commercial service scale or first-AI-in-space verification; ambiguous Gemini/Gemma wording omitted.

claims.title: Suncatcher ground optical bench result
claims.statement: The study reports 800 Gbit/s one-way transfer on a short free-space bench path, with 1.6 Tbit/s labeled bidirectional.
claims.denominator: one direction of tested short free-space path
claims.limitations: Bidirectional aggregate is a different metric; does not establish ground contact availability or a flight-qualified network.

claims.title: TBIRD demonstrated peak downlink rate
claims.statement: NASA reports a 200 Gbit/s peak downlink rate in the TBIRD demonstration.
claims.scope: Peak within an on-orbit communication demonstration
claims.limitations: Not a continuous daily rate; contact duration and useful delivered volume are separately recorded.

claims.title: TBIRD delivered bytes in one pass
claims.statement: NASA reports 4.8 TB of error-free data delivered in one five-minute pass in June 2023.
claims.scope: Measured pass payload as reported by NASA
claims.limitations: Distinct from multiplying peak bit rate by the full contact duration; not all-day sustained service.

claims.title: Suncatcher radiation-test qualifications
claims.statement: The study reports HBM-test irregularities after about 2 krad(Si), while other tests continued to a 15 krad(Si) maximum on one chip.
claims.metric: Reported onset of HBM stress-test irregularities
claims.denominator: tested device and specified proton-beam conditions
claims.limitations: Maximum-dose survival is not complete mission qualification or single-event immunity; one-chip sample and test scope limit generalization.

claims.title: Conditional launch-price projection
claims.statement: The study projects launch prices near or below $200/kg by the mid-2030s under learning-curve and launch-growth assumptions.
claims.denominator: mass launched to LEO under the study assumptions
claims.limitations: Not a current price, guaranteed forecast or complete system-cost comparison; spacecraft and operational costs remain outside this component.

claims.title: Google’s dated prototype-mission plan
claims.statement: Google’s November 2025 announcement targets two prototype satellites with Planet for early 2027.
claims.limitations: No launch completion inferred; simulation and bench evidence remain separate.

claims.title: Capacity planning versus customer allocation
claims.statement: TSMC’s 2025 annual report describes planning capacity with customers and their customers.
claims.limitations: Does not reveal customer queues, allocated shares or a transferable package-output-per-month default.
